# Sources RAG entry point

Answer only from the assigned MCP dataset.

The dataset contains source records (with `path` `sources`): original evidence from documents, messages, meetings, and task systems. Use these records to answer and cite.

## Retrieval

The `mcp__tl-v1__ragflow_retrieval` tool is deferred. Load it first with ToolSearch using the query `select:mcp__tl-v1__ragflow_retrieval`.

On every retrieval, pass only the dataset ID assigned to this arm and use `metadata_condition` to restrict `path` to `sources`. Use concrete identifiers and topic terms from the question, and retrieve further evidence as needed to answer all material parts.

Pass these values on every `ragflow_retrieval` call, and do not vary them between calls:

```
page_size: 10
vector_similarity_weight: 0.3
similarity_threshold: 0.2
top_k: 1024
keyword: false
```

If the retrieved sources do not support an answer, say so. Cite the source records used for the answer.

Return the complete answer in the final response. Your final response IS the deliverable — it must contain the full answer text verbatim, not a summary or a pointer to work done.

---

Several streams remain blocked while others are only reopened. As of **2026-09-22**, what work can still advance in parallel, what cannot progress until an external dependency moves, and what release-checklist work is gated on packaging and Windows signing?

Use only `tl-v1` MCP with `d13efb7c8a9a11f197db2303d7337e37` dataset to answer. Do not use web, local files, memory, or any other MCP dataset.

Use when user wants to write documentation, proposals, technical specs, decision docs, or similar structured content. This workflow helps users efficiently transfer context, refine content through iteration, and verify the doc works for readers. Trigger when user mentions writing docs, creating proposals, drafting specs, or similar documentation tasks.
- anthropic-skills:docx: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx files) or Word templates (.dotx files). Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, headings, page numbers, or letterheads. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, performing find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a 'report', 'memo', 'letter', 'template', or similar deliverable as a Word or .docx file, use this skill. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or general coding tasks unrelated to document generation.
- anthropic-skills:morning: Render the user's morning brief as a styled HTML artifact, or set it up as a recurring weekday task. Use only when the user explicitly asks to run, see, or set up their morning brief, or if they invoke /morning by name. A question about their day, schedule, or calendar is not by itself a request for the brief; answer it directly instead.
- anthropic-skills:pdf: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. This includes reading or extracting text/tables from PDFs, combining or merging multiple PDFs into one, splitting PDFs apart, rotating pages, adding watermarks, creating new PDFs, filling PDF forms, encrypting/decrypting PDFs, extracting images, and OCR on scanned PDFs to make them searchable. - anthropic-skills:pptx: Use this skill any time a .pptx or .potx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx or .potx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email or summary); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates (.potx), layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user mentions "deck," "slides," "presentation," or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. If a .pptx or .potx file needs to be opened, created, or touched, use this skill.
- anthropic-skills:schedule: Create or update a scheduled task that runs automatically. Use when the user says things like "every day", "each morning", "remind me in an hour", "run this at noon", or wants to reschedule an existing task.
- anthropic-skills:setup-cowork: Guided Cowork setup — install role-matched plugins, connect your tools, try a skill.
- anthropic-skills:skill-creator: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.
- anthropic-skills:xlsx: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Trigger especially when the user references a spreadsheet file by name or path — even casually (like "the xlsx in my downloads") — and wants something done to it or produced from it. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved.

- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, or updating and republishing itself. ## Original Finding: Ghostscript (AGPLv3)

The initial audit flagged `Ghostscript`, used by the `rasterizer` module for PDF-to-image conversion, as AGPLv3-licensed — on the corporate license blacklist because of its viral copyleft terms for any binary distributed to partner sites.

**Source ID**: SRC-GDOC-41

# Dependency Inventory: License Compliance Audit (Q3) — Reopened

**Owner**: Diana

**Document Key**: DOC-2041

**Last Updated**: 2026-08-21 (reflects reopen activity through 2026-08-15)

## First Remediation and Reopen

# Queue Design Review: Async Batch Processing — Concurrency Block

**Owner**: Bob

**Document Key**: DOC-2050

**Last Updated**: 2026-09-04 (retrospective, covers 2026-08-25)

## Worker Management Decision

Retrospective note on the concurrency block confirmed 2026-08-25. For large-scale redaction jobs, the batch API moved from a synchronous blocking loop to an `asyncio`-driven queue: a single producer walks the file system and pushes document tasks, while a fixed pool of async workers pulls from the queue and orchestrates I/O against the redaction engine, built on top of the already-completed multi-threaded worker pool (T026).

**Source ID**: SRC-GDOC-50

# Queue Design Review: Async Batch Processing — Concurrency Block

**Owner**: Bob

**Document Key**: DOC-2050

**Last Updated**: 2026-09-04 (retrospective, covers 2026-08-25)

## Ordering & Race Risk

Because documents vary widely in size, workers finish out of order. When multiple workers append to the same shared results manifest concurrently, writes can interleave and corrupt the JSON structure.

**Source ID**: SRC-GDOC-50

# Queue Design Review: Async Batch Processing — Concurrency Block

**Owner**: Bob

**Document Key**: DOC-2050

**Last Updated**: 2026-09-04 (retrospective, covers 2026-08-25)

## Update: Confirmed I/O Race, Throughput Regression

Concurrency testing on 2026-08-25 confirmed the race is real, not just theoretical: under concurrent load, the race condition measurably cuts batch throughput by roughly 10% compared to the expected async speedup, because workers end up retrying/serializing around the corrupted-write recovery path. This is now blocking further rollout of the async scheduler.

**Source ID**: SRC-GDOC-50

# Queue Design Review: Async Batch Processing — Concurrency Block

**Owner**: Bob

**Document Key**: DOC-2050

**Last Updated**: 2026-09-04 (retrospective, covers 2026-08-25)

## Status

T037 is **Blocked** on resolving the manifest-write race before the async scheduler can be considered production-ready; the throughput regression it causes depends directly on how the T026 worker pool's result-writing is serialized.

# Crypto Sign-off: AES-256 At-Rest Encryption Pipeline

**Owner**: Diana

**Document Key**: DOC-2035

**Last Updated**: 2026-08-07

## Sign-off Basis

Security sign-off on the AES-256 at-rest pipeline was withheld until the fail-closed deletion behavior for interrupted redaction runs (T015) was confirmed Completed — an unencrypted partial output left on disk after a crash would have undermined the encryption guarantee entirely. With that dependency cleared, the sign-off proceeded against the pipeline as implemented.

**Source ID**: SRC-GDOC-35

# Crypto Sign-off: AES-256 At-Rest Encryption Pipeline

**Owner**: Diana

**Document Key**: DOC-2035

**Last Updated**: 2026-08-07

## What Was Reviewed

- AES-256-GCM authenticated encryption applied to every redacted output file before it is written to its final location.

- Key handling confined to process memory; no plaintext key material written to disk or logs.

- Confirmed the pipeline degrades safely (refuses to write plaintext) if key material is unavailable, consistent with the fail-closed contract from T015.

**Source ID**: SRC-GDOC-35

# Crypto Sign-off: AES-256 At-Rest Encryption Pipeline

**Owner**: Diana

**Document Key**: DOC-2035

**Last Updated**: 2026-08-07

## Follow-up Noted at Sign-off

On machines without a hardware TPM, the volume key is still derived from a user passphrase via PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 at 100k iterations. This is not a blocker for the AES-256 pipeline sign-off itself, but Diana flagged it as a hardening follow-up: moving to Argon2id would meaningfully raise the cost of offline brute-force against weak passphrases on non-TPM hardware.

*Status*: AES-256 at-rest pipeline signed off as Completed. Passphrase-derived key hardening (Argon2id) tracked separately as a pre-v1.0 hardening item, not a sign-off condition.

# Queue Design Review: Async Batch Processing — Concurrency Block

**Owner**: Bob

**Document Key**: DOC-2050

**Last Updated**: 2026-09-04 (retrospective, covers 2026-08-25)

## Worker Management Decision

Retrospective note on the concurrency block confirmed 2026-08-25. For large-scale redaction jobs, the batch API moved from a synchronous blocking loop to an `asyncio`-driven queue: a single producer walks the file system and pushes document tasks, while a fixed pool of async workers pulls from the queue and orchestrates I/O against the redaction engine, built on top of the already-completed multi-threaded worker pool (T026).

**Source ID**: SRC-GDOC-50

# Queue Design Review: Async Batch Processing — Concurrency Block

**Owner**: Bob

**Document Key**: DOC-2050

**Last Updated**: 2026-09-04 (retrospective, covers 2026-08-25)

## Ordering & Race Risk

Because documents vary widely in size, workers finish out of order. When multiple workers append to the same shared results manifest concurrently, writes can interleave and corrupt the JSON structure.

**Source ID**: SRC-GDOC-50

# Queue Design Review: Async Batch Processing — Concurrency Block

**Owner**: Bob

**Document Key**: DOC-2050

**Last Updated**: 2026-09-04 (retrospective, covers 2026-08-25)

## Update: Confirmed I/O Race, Throughput Regression

Concurrency testing on 2026-08-25 confirmed the race is real, not just theoretical: under concurrent load, the race condition measurably cuts batch throughput by roughly 10% compared to the expected async speedup, because workers end up retrying/serializing around the corrupted-write recovery path. This is now blocking further rollout of the async scheduler.

**Source ID**: SRC-GDOC-50

# Queue Design Review: Async Batch Processing — Concurrency Block

**Owner**: Bob

**Document Key**: DOC-2050

**Last Updated**: 2026-09-04 (retrospective, covers 2026-08-25)

# Privacy Design Note: Telemetry Opt-Out Flag Semantics

**Owner**: Diana

**Document Key**: DOC-2051

**Last Updated**: 2026-09-06

## Opt-Out Behaviour Designed

The CLI and API collect anonymous usage metrics (pages processed, OCR fallback rate) to help tune the detection engine. Setting `CIPHER_TELEMETRY=0`, or the equivalent GUI toggle, is designed to immediately stop all outbound telemetry traffic to the metrics endpoint.

**Source ID**: SRC-GDOC-51

# Privacy Design Note: Telemetry Opt-Out Flag Semantics

**Owner**: Diana

**Document Key**: DOC-2051

**Last Updated**: 2026-09-06

## Design-Time Issue Found and Patched: Pending-Queue Leak

While designing the flag semantics, testing surfaced that the opt-out flag blocked network egress correctly, but the `TelemetryLogger` kept writing event payloads to a local SQLite queue regardless. That meant re-enabling telemetry later would flush the entire backlog accumulated during the opt-out period, including events the user believed were never being recorded. The logger was patched to a no-op backend when opted out, closing that gap before the flag semantics were finalized.

**Source ID**: SRC-GDOC-51

# Privacy Design Note: Telemetry Opt-Out Flag Semantics

**Owner**: Diana

**Document Key**: DOC-2051

**Last Updated**: 2026-09-06

## Verification (Retrospective)

A network trace on 2026-08-24 confirmed zero outbound telemetry traffic once the opt-out flag is set, closing the CLI-side verification as Completed.

**Source ID**: SRC-GDOC-51

# Privacy Design Note: Telemetry Opt-Out Flag Semantics

**Owner**: Diana

**Document Key**: DOC-2051

**Last Updated**: 2026-09-06

## Remaining Limitation

The third-party Electron crash reporter (Sentry) has not been audited for whether it independently respects the opt-out environment variable or requires its own disable hook for minidump uploads.

*Note*: CLI-side telemetry opt-out is verified. Full privacy compliance for air-gapped/opt-out users cannot be claimed until the Sentry crash-reporter path is audited separately.

Post-merge testing on files at and above 2GB surfaced a memory leak: buffers allocated for each chunk were not being released once the chunk finished processing, so peak memory climbed roughly linearly with file size instead of staying bounded by the chunk size. This defeated the point of chunking for the largest files, and the task was reopened as Active (Reopened).

# Design Note: Large File Chunking Strategy

**Owner**: Charlie

**Document Key**: DOC-2025

**Last Updated**: 2026-08-14

## The Failure Mode

When processing massive multi-GB PDF documents (e.g., a 4,000-page merged archive), the loader attempts to load the entire document tree into RAM. For files exceeding 2GB, this consistently results in an `OOMKilled` exception in our standard 4GB Docker containers.

**Source ID**: SRC-GDOC-25

# Design Note: Large File Chunking Strategy

**Owner**: Charlie

**Document Key**: DOC-2025

**Last Updated**: 2026-08-14

## Chunking Implementation

We implemented and merged a "Stream-and-Split" pre-processing layer today. 

1. The CLI reads the source PDF in 100-page blocks.

2. Each block is saved as a temporary sub-document (`doc_part_1.pdf`, `doc_part_2.pdf`).

3. The worker pool processes these sub-documents independently.

4. A post-processing step merges the redacted sub-documents back into a single final PDF.

**Source ID**: SRC-GDOC-25

# Design Note: Large File Chunking Strategy

**Owner**: Charlie

**Document Key**: DOC-2025

**Last Updated**: 2026-08-14

## Ordering and Memory Trade-off

This approach solves the RAM issue but introduces a significant disk I/O and ordering overhead. Re-merging the PDFs requires careful tracking of the chunk sequence. Furthermore, if a regex pattern was supposed to match across a page boundary (e.g., a sentence split across pages 100 and 101), the chunking will break the match. We are trading context-awareness for memory stability.

*Pending*: We need to run a stress test with a 10,000-page document to verify if the final re-merge step (which also uses RAM) re-introduces the OOM crash.

**[2026-06-12 13:17] Charlie**: Perfect. :lock:

**[2026-06-12 13:19] Alice**: Thanks.

**[2026-07-16 09:30] Diana**: QA pass on fail-closed is done — confirmed no output file gets written on failure and the temp files get securely deleted. Signing off before the encryption and offline work start relying on this.

I'm reviewing the key blockers we're facing. There's a critical issue with high-DPI PDF coordinate scaling that's stuck waiting on an upstream library fix in pdf-lib-core—specifically around nested Form XObjects and coordinate transforms. The maintainers haven't responded yet, and since it's deep in their C++ implementation, we can't patch it ourselves. The flattening workaround didn't pan out either.

We're also waiting on an unmerged PR in pdfminer.six for coordinate drift in multi-page PDFs, and we can't fork it. Windows code-signing is blocked on procurement of a certificate with no firm timeline, though the packaging work is done. On the library side, Charlie's searching for an Apache or MIT-licensed PDF parser as a replacement, and Evan's still tracing the provenance of Tesseract's tessdata.

Internally, we're stuck on the AES-256 encryption path for the handshake, an I/O race condition in the async batch scheduler with multi-thread pool writes, and the offline auth key rotation which fundamentally requires network access in an air-gapped environment.

Several items can move forward in parallel: Charlie's refactoring the large-file stream chunking with per-chunk buffer releases and testing against a 2.3GB sample; Diana's wiring the OCR fallback with per-page multiprocessing and confidence tuning into the scan pipeline; Bob's got another pass on the audit-trail logging to align CLI records with the schema; Evan's still working through Python site-packages cleanup and CVE scan triggers for the Docker image; the redaction profile export schema design is done and waiting on endpoint implementation; and there's static analysis work queued up.

On the release side, the checklist is active with most dependencies completed, but the Docker packaging work is still reopened and blocking—that's one of two named gates along with Windows code-signing. Meanwhile, the license-compliance parser evaluation can proceed pending external library confirmation, release notes are being drafted in parallel, the telemetry opt-out is verified on the CLI side with the Sentry crash-reporter audit as separate work, and there's follow-up patching needed on a PDF loader memory leak. So T011 is blocked by both T005 (Docker packaging and CVE verification) and T029 (Windows signing), which directly answers what release-checklist work depends on those two areas.

## Answer

### Snapshot as of 2026-09-22

The board splits three ways: streams that are genuinely unblocked and can run concurrently, streams held by a dependency the team does not control, and the v1.0 release checklist, which is pinned by two named gates plus a live audit-log mismatch.

---

### 1. Work that can still advance in parallel

**Docker image slim-down / CVE remediation (T005, CIPH-15 — Active (Reopened), Evan).** Reopened 2026-06-25 after the image measured 2.1GB. Multi-stage build, Alpine base swap, and removal of unused OCR/runtime packages are all done; the 2026-08-12 verification still showed the image over the ~450MB target with CVE verification failing. Evan named the remaining work himself: fluff still in the Python site-packages layer, and chasing down what trips the CVE scan. Nothing external gates this — it is engineering effort that can proceed today. *(SRC-CU-CIPH-15, SRC-SLACK-06, SRC-GDOC-05)*

**Large-file stream chunking buffer-release refactor (T041, CIPH-41 — Active (Reopened), Charlie).** Chunking merged to mainline 2026-08-16, then reopened when files at and above 2GB leaked memory because per-chunk buffers were not released. Charlie is refactoring the stream-chunk handler to release eagerly after each chunk; a 2.3GB local sample already shows flat memory instead of the previous linear climb, but the fix is not yet validated against the full large-file corpus. Independent of every blocked stream. *(SRC-GDOC-42, SRC-SLACK-44, SRC-CU-CIPH-41)*

**Memory-leak patching in the PDF loader.** The identification pass (Bob, from 2026-08-17; unblocked 2026-08-21 when Charlie switched to stdlib `tracemalloc` after the usual profiler proved unavailable in the offline lab) traced retained allocations to the loader's page-buffer handling across chunk boundaries. Patching the loader is explicitly scoped as separate follow-up work and can run. *(SRC-GDOC-27)*

**Audit-trail logging (T016, CIPH-26 — Active, Diana/Bob).** Loader refactor, SHA-256 input hashing, schema definition, and CLI wiring (2026-09-10) are all done. Verification on 2026-09-18 found CLI-emitted records inconsistent with the defined schema. Bob has "another pass queued." Charlie confirmed at the 2026-09-15 audit that this is schema-versus-emitted-records, **not** a packaging problem — so it advances independently of the packaging and signing gates, even though it is itself a release blocker. *(SRC-CU-CIPH-26, SRC-MEET-10)*

**OCR fallback (CIPH-18 — Active, Charlie).** Tesseract POC succeeded; the page-serial loop bottleneck was addressed with a per-page multiprocessing pool and retuned confidence thresholds. Diana has begun wiring OCR fallback output into the scan pipeline while parallelization work continues. Two people working concurrently on the same stream. *(SRC-CU-CIPH-18)*

**License-compliance parser search (Charlie).** The Ghostscript (AGPLv3) swap was reopened when the replacement parser turned out to also be AGPL — same license category, one layer down. Charlie is comparing Apache 2.0 / MIT candidates against the rasterizer module's requirements; Alice named this the priority at the 2026-08-15 sync. The evaluation work proceeds now, though *confirming* a replacement depends on a suitable library existing. *(SRC-GDOC-41, SRC-MEET-08)*

**Exportable redaction-profile schema (T032).** Design pass complete as of 2026-08-12; implementing the schema-export API and verifying it against the REST contract remain open and unclaimed. *(SRC-GDOC-26)*

**Static-linking study for the air-gapped local runtime (Evan).** Full-static versus hybrid bundling of `re2` and the C dependencies; tracked by the release checklist alongside the Docker slim-down. *(SRC-SLACK-14)*

**Sentry crash-reporter privacy audit.** CLI-side telemetry opt-out was verified Completed by network trace on 2026-08-24; the third-party Electron crash reporter has not been audited for whether it independently respects the opt-out variable. Separate, actionable. *(SRC-GDOC-51)*

**Release notes.** Explicitly drafted in parallel while the gates stayed open — the sources record this as accepted practice, not a violation. *(SRC-CU-CIPH-21)*

---

### 2. Work that cannot progress until an external dependency moves

**High-DPI PDF coordinate scaling (T036, CIPH-46 — Blocked, Charlie).** Charlie's rotation fix works for simple cases but breaks completely on documents with nested Form XObjects. Root cause is a known bug in the upstream rendering library `pdf-lib-core` — how it handles XObject coordinates when a parent transform is applied. Charlie's assessment: "It's deep in their C++ core." He opened an issue with the upstream maintainers and they have not responded. The PDF-flattening workaround Evan proposed would blow up file size and risk losing text layers, so it was not adopted. Alice's 2026-09-10 call was to leave it blocked and decide whether to ship with the limitation or replace the rendering library entirely; Diana noted it affects only a small subset of complex documents and should be documented as a known issue. Still listed as open at the 2026-09-15 pre-release audit. *(SRC-SLACK-58, SRC-CU-CIPH-46, SRC-GDOC-49, SRC-MEET-10)*

**Coordinate/offset drift in multi-page PDFs (CIPH-17 — Blocked, Charlie).** Traced to whitespace handling in upstream `pdfminer.six`, pending PR #992. Charlie re-checked on 2026-09-10: still unmerged, no maintainer movement. Forking pdfminer.six was formally evaluated and rejected on 2026-08-20 — long-term maintenance risk of owning a PDF parser exceeds the cost of waiting. Alice flagged this as "a real risk for the v1.0 timeline"; Charlie's position was he would rather eat the delay. No local workaround adopted. *(SRC-SLACK-07, SRC-CU-CIPH-17)*

**Windows code-signing (T029, CIPH-39 — Active, Evan).** Gated on procurement, not engineering. Evan is unambiguous: "this isn't something we can work around on the engineering side, we need the certificate." As of 2026-08-15 he was still waiting on procurement with no firm timeline. Alice took the action to chase the certificate process. *(SRC-SLACK-37, SRC-GDOC-39, SRC-MEET-08)*

**Tesseract `eng.traineddata` provenance.** A separate, lower-priority open item pending Evan's trace of the `tessdata_best` training-corpus provenance against public-domain/CC0 — dependent on an external community repository's records. *(SRC-GDOC-41)*

*Distinguish these from internally blocked streams,* which are stuck but not on an outside party:
- **Authenticated node-sync handshake (CIPH-34 — Blocked, reopened 2026-09-22).** Diana reopened it that morning: over a simulated high-latency link the handshake times out and never completes, degrading as the link slows. Bob traced it to the AES-256 pipeline on the output path adding per-packet overhead that pushes the exchange past the timeout window. Evan rejected a timeout bump as concealment ("if the link is slow enough, we still fail"), and Bob has no fix that preserves the current exchange. Alice's ruling: stays blocked, no workaround invented in the meeting; revisit when the crypto path moves. Diana left the high-latency repro in place. *(SRC-SLACK-27, SRC-MEET-11, SRC-CU-CIPH-34)*
- **Async batch job scheduler (T037, CIPH-47 — Blocked, Bob).** Concurrent async workers sharing I/O with the existing multi-threaded pool corrupt the shared results manifest; recovery-path retries cut throughput ~10% versus the sync baseline. Alice: "A 10% hit is not shippable." *(SRC-CU-CIPH-47, SRC-SLACK-61, SRC-GDOC-50)*
- **Offline auth with key rotation (CIPH-29 — Blocked, High, Diana).** Key rotation cannot complete without network access in an air-gapped setting; no resolution found. *(SRC-CU-CIPH-29)*

---

### 3. Release-checklist work gated on packaging and Windows signing

**T011 / CIPH-21 "Release v1.0 Gates" is Active, owner Evan, with a security-gate hold placed by Diana.**

The original dependency set (T001–T006, T010) is six-sevenths satisfied — Core Redaction Engine, Financial Regex Detection, Batch CLI, REST API Endpoints, Redaction Policy Config, and Security Audit are all Completed. **T005 Docker Packaging is the one unmet dependency from that original list.**

Two gates hold the checklist:

| Gate | Nature of block | Status |
|---|---|---|
| **T005 — Docker image slim-down / CVE** | Packaging. Image over ~450MB target; CVE verification failing | Active (Reopened) since 2026-06-25 |
| **T029 — Windows Defender/SmartScreen code-signing** | Procurement, not engineering | Active; certificate not procured |

**The critical distinction on the Windows side: packaging is no longer the blocker there.** The backslash path-handling defects that broke Windows builds were fixed 2026-08-10, and a build artifact was successfully produced 2026-08-12 — it installs on a Windows box and passes the same sanity checks run on Linux. Evan drew the line explicitly at the time: the engineering work for the Windows build is complete, but code-signing is a separate item not yet started, so he would not call the whole thing closed. Procuring a code-signing certificate and wiring signing into the release build step is "the only remaining item" before T029 clears — and, by extension, before T011 clears, since the checklist holds on this exact signing gap alongside the T005 image slim-down.

So the packaging half of the gating is **entirely Docker**, not Windows. The unsigned artifact triggers SmartScreen warnings and Defender flagging; site IT policies commonly block unsigned binaries outright, which would prevent installation on target deployment workstations without a manual security-policy override.

**Beyond the two formal gates,** the 2026-09-15 pre-release audit added the audit-log schema mismatch as a visible release blocker — Diana is keeping that gate red until schema and emitted records match — and kept the upstream high-DPI bug on the board. Evan's summary of the stack: "Release isn't opening with any of those unresolved." Alice closed the meeting with "No one closes those today."

---

### Bottom line

Roughly nine streams can run concurrently right now, and they cluster on the two people with unblocked capacity: Evan on Docker size/CVE and static linking, Charlie on the buffer-release refactor, OCR parallelization, and the license-safe parser search, with Bob on the audit-schema pass and loader leak patch. Four items wait on outsiders — two upstream PDF libraries (`pdf-lib-core` unresponsive, `pdfminer.six` #992 unmerged), a code-signing certificate stuck in procurement, and Tesseract model provenance. Release v1.0 opens on exactly two gates, and only one of them (Docker) is engineering-addressable; the other (Windows signing) will move when procurement does, no sooner.
